name: Shoutem
tagline: Drag-and-drop builder that turns content and screens into native iOS and Android apps.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: The part Shoutem sells as magic, assembling tab bars, content lists, event screens and a push feed, is exactly what a coding agent is good at. One session of Expo and TypeScript gets you a running app on your own phone with your own content, no monthly fee. What you do not get in that session is the boring half: signing certificates, App Store and Play review, OTA updates, push delivery infra, and a web dashboard a non-technical person can edit content in. If the app is for you and your pocket, build it. If it is for a client who will want copy changes every Tuesday, the builder is earning its money.
coreLoopDIY: An Expo app that renders your own screens and content from local JSON or a Git-backed feed, runs on your phone, and ships updates when you rebuild.
requirements: a phone with Expo Go, or Xcode/Android Studio for a real build
paid Apple and Google developer accounts if you ever want store distribution
whatYouLose: App Store and Play submission handled for you, including signing, certificates and review churn
A visual editor a non-developer can use to change screens and content
Hosted CMS so content edits do not require a rebuild
Managed push notifications with segmentation and delivery reporting
Prebuilt templates and integrations for things like events, commerce and social feeds
moatNotes: The build and release pipeline is the actual product. Nobody pays a monthly fee for a tab bar.
whyPeopleStillPay: Mostly agencies and small businesses who do not want to learn what a provisioning profile is. Shoutem's value is that someone else owns the build servers, the store submissions, the push gateway and a dashboard the client can poke at without breaking anything. A DIY Expo app is genuinely better for one technical person who wants one app, and genuinely worse the moment a second non-technical person needs to edit it or the thing has to exist on two app stores forever.
notes: Easy to build, annoying to ship: the gap between localhost and TestFlight is where the subscription lives.
prompt:
Build a personal mobile app scaffold I can run on my own phone, no app-builder SaaS involved.

Stack, non negotiable:
- Expo (managed workflow) with React Native and TypeScript
- expo-router for file based navigation
- A bottom tab bar with four tabs: Home, Content, Events, About
- Content comes from local files in /content as JSON plus Markdown bodies, parsed at build time, no backend
- react-native-markdown-display for rendering article bodies
- Theme in a single theme.ts file: colors, spacing, type scale. One light theme, no theme switcher.

What to build:
1. /content/config.json holds app name, tagline, accent color, and the tab list.
2. /content/posts/*.md with frontmatter (title, date, summary, image). Content tab shows a list, tapping opens a detail screen.
3. /content/events.json with title, start date, location, description. Events tab shows upcoming first, past collapsed at the bottom.
4. Home tab shows the three newest posts and the next event in cards.
5. About tab renders /content/about.md plus a list of external links that open in the system browser.
6. Pull to refresh that just re-reads the bundled content so the gesture is not a lie.
7. Graceful empty states for every list.

Out of scope, do not build or stub: user accounts, analytics, telemetry, push notifications, in-app purchases, a CMS, admin UI, any network calls at all.

Also produce:
- README with run instructions for Expo Go on iOS and Android
- A short section in the README listing the exact extra steps needed for real store distribution (dev accounts, EAS build, signing), clearly marked as not done
- .env.example only if a key is genuinely needed, otherwise do not create one

Keep it to as few files as the structure allows. Run it and fix anything that errors before you hand it back.
